segments.narration: Liquid electric blue fire flows down an Indonesian mountain every night. It looks like glowing neon blue lava spilling into the dark valley below. For decades, travelers swore the mountain was cursed by glowing spirits.
segments.visual_query: kawah ijen blue fire indonesia night

segments.narration: Locals called it the devil’s light, watching bright cobalt streams snake through the rock. The strange glow is completely invisible by day, but as soon as the sun dips, the landscape ignites. What kind of lava glows electric blue?
segments.visual_query: kawah ijen crater lake indonesia darkness

segments.narration: The reality is even wilder—because that blue liquid isn't lava at all. High inside the crater of Kawah Ijen, massive pockets of high-pressure sulfuric gas leak out through deep cracks in the rock.
segments.visual_query: kawah ijen sulfuric gas crater indonesia

segments.narration: When those pressurized gases meet oxygen at temperatures up to six hundred degrees, they burst into intense blue flames, with condensing gas creating burning liquid sulfur that flows down the slopes.
segments.visual_query: kawah ijen burning sulfur flames indonesia

segments.narration: So the mountain isn't spewing blue magma—it's literally leaking liquid fire.
segments.visual_query: kawah ijen volcano slopes indonesia night

accuracy_flags.claim: Sulfuric gas ignites upon contact with oxygen at temperatures exceeding six hundred degrees Celsius.
accuracy_flags.note: The reference text specifies that the sulfuric gas emerges at temperatures up to 600 °C (1,112 °F), not exceeding or above 600 °C.
